title: Reproductive, Placental, and Breast Embryology
subject: Reproductive System (REPR)
author: Dr. Sharilyn Rennie

overview.intro: This chapter follows one bipotential gonad, two pairs of ducts, and one set of external primordia as they become male or female organs, then covers descent of the testis, formation of the placenta and umbilical cord, and development of the breast. Board questions usually give a karyotype, a missing hormone or enzyme, or a malformation and ask you to predict the anatomy. The reasoning rests on a short chain: SRY decides the gonad, the gonad's hormones decide the ducts and genitalia, and each embryonic step that fails leaves a predictable defect. Learn which cell makes which signal and which structure that signal builds or removes.

Defects in steroidogenesis, 5-alpha-reductase, or the androgen receptor alter external and internal anatomy in predictable ways.
Sex chromosome aneuploidy and SRY translocation or deletion explain most disorders of gonadal development.

connections.to: Congenital reproductive diseases (RE-13-C) and placental disease (RE-13-H)

The path of testicular descent creates the inguinal canal, the spermatic cord coverings, and the gonadal blood supply and lymph drainage.

sections.title: SRY and determination of the gonad

blocks.text: The gonad begins in week 5 as the genital (gonadal) ridge, a thickening of coelomic epithelium and underlying intermediate mesoderm on the medial side of the mesonephros. Primordial germ cells, which arise in the epiblast and gather in the yolk sac wall, migrate along the dorsal mesentery of the hindgut and enter the ridges in week 6. Epithelial cells proliferate into primitive sex cords around the germ cells. Until about week 7 the gonad is bipotential: its supporting cells can become Sertoli cells or granulosa cells, and both duct pairs are present.

SRY (sex-determining region Y) lies on the short arm of the Y chromosome, near the boundary of the pseudoautosomal region. It encodes a transcription factor with an HMG DNA-binding domain, also called testis-determining factor. SRY acts in the supporting cells at about week 7, where it switches on SOX9. SOX9 then maintains its own expression through a positive feedback loop involving FGF9 and prostaglandin D2, which is why the gonad stays committed once SOX9 is established. SOX9-positive cells become Sertoli cells, which enclose the germ cells in testis (seminiferous) cords, a dense tunica albuginea forms beneath the surface, and Sertoli cell signals induce interstitial mesenchyme to become Leydig cells. The Sertoli cell is the organizer of the testis, and every later male step depends on it.

Without SRY, the supporting cells become granulosa cells, the cords break into clusters around oogonia in the cortex, and an ovary forms. The ovary is often called the default pathway, but it is actively maintained by WNT4, RSPO1 with beta-catenin, and FOXL2, which repress SOX9. Ovarian maintenance also needs two X chromosomes: in 45,X Turner syndrome oocytes are lost by apoptosis and the ovaries become fibrous streaks.

Prediction follows one rule: SRY decides the gonad, whatever the rest of the karyotype. A 46,XY embryo with an SRY deletion or inactivating mutation forms streak gonads (complete gonadal dysgenesis, Swyer syndrome). Streaks make neither AMH nor testosterone, so the Mullerian ducts persist, the Wolffian ducts regress, and the external genitalia are female. Puberty does not occur because there is no ovarian estrogen, and streak gonads containing Y material carry a high risk of gonadoblastoma and dysgerminoma. A 46,XX embryo with SRY translocated to an X chromosome, usually by abnormal X and Y exchange during paternal meiosis, forms testes and a male phenotype. The testes are small and produce no sperm because the azoospermia factor (AZF) genes on the long arm of the Y are absent, and gonadotropins are high (hypergonadotropic hypogonadism).

blocks.caption: The presence of SRY, not the number of X chromosomes, decides whether a testis forms. Ducts and genitalia then follow the gonad's hormones.

blocks.predict: A 46,XX man has small firm testes, no uterus, and azoospermia. Did his fetal gonads make AMH, and why is he infertile?
blocks.explain: Yes. The translocated SRY made Sertoli cells, which secreted AMH and removed the Mullerian ducts, and Leydig cell androgens masculinized him. Sperm are absent because the AZF spermatogenesis genes on the long arm of the Y were not translocated with SRY.

sections.title: AMH, testosterone, and DHT: three separate male signals

blocks.text: Once a testis exists, two cell types and one enzyme carry out the rest of male development. Each signal acts on a different target, so each can fail alone, and most board questions on disorders of sex development depend on that independence.

blocks.title: The three male signals
cols: If it fails in a 46,XY fetus
rows: Uterus and tubes persist in a virilized male (persistent Mullerian duct syndrome)
Leydig cells, driven by placental hCG, later fetal LH
Epididymis, ductus deferens, seminal vesicle, ejaculatory duct
Testosterone converted by 5-alpha-reductase type 2 in target tissue
Genital tubercle, urogenital folds, labioscrotal swellings, urogenital sinus
Ambiguous or female external genitalia; small or absent prostate
blocks.caption: AMH removes, testosterone keeps, and DHT builds. Testosterone and DHT act through the same androgen receptor.

blocks.text: AMH, a TGF-beta family glycoprotein, binds AMH receptor type 2 on the mesenchyme surrounding each paramesonephric duct, which triggers apoptosis of the duct epithelium. The duct responds only during a short window, about weeks 8 to 10, so AMH arriving later cannot remove it. Testosterone stabilizes the mesonephric duct by acting locally: it diffuses from the testis to the duct on the same side at a concentration far above plasma levels. That is why a 46,XX fetus exposed to adrenal androgens in 21-hydroxylase deficiency has virilized external genitalia but no Wolffian derivatives, and why an individual with a testis on one side and an ovary on the other has male ducts only on the testis side.

Genital skin and the urogenital sinus express 5-alpha-reductase type 2. DHT binds the androgen receptor with higher affinity and dissociates more slowly than testosterone, amplifying the signal in tissues that are far from the testis. DHT drives growth of the genital tubercle, fusion of the urogenital folds and labioscrotal swellings, and budding of the prostate from urogenital sinus endoderm.

In the female, the absence of AMH lets the paramesonephric ducts persist, and the absence of testosterone lets the mesonephric ducts regress, leaving remnants such as the epoophoron and the Gartner duct, which can form a cyst in the lateral vaginal wall. Female ducts and external genitalia need no gonadal hormone, so a fetus with no functioning gonads develops female anatomy.

blocks.caption: Each arrow is a separate gene product, so a single defect stops the chain at a predictable point.

blocks.title: Three 46,XY patients, three defects
blocks.text: Patient A has female external genitalia, a short blind vagina, no uterus, and inguinal testes. Testes formed and AMH removed the uterus, but neither testosterone nor DHT acted: complete androgen insensitivity (androgen receptor defect). Breasts develop at puberty because abundant testosterone is aromatized to estradiol. Patient B has ambiguous genitalia at birth, a normal epididymis and ductus deferens, and virilizes at puberty. Testosterone acted on the Wolffian ducts but DHT was lacking: 5-alpha-reductase type 2 deficiency. Patient C is a normally virilized male whose uterus and tubes are found during inguinal surgery. Androgens worked but AMH did not: a defect in AMH or its receptor. For each case, ask which structure is present, then which hormone builds or removes it.

sections.title: Paramesonephric ducts and uterine fusion anomalies

blocks.text: The paramesonephric ducts form around week 6 as longitudinal invaginations of coelomic epithelium on the lateral surface of each mesonephros. Their cranial ends stay open to the coelomic cavity, and their caudal growth follows the adjacent mesonephric duct, which acts as a guide. Each duct runs downward, crosses ventral to the mesonephric duct, and meets its partner in the midline.

The cranial, unfused parts become the uterine tubes, with the open ends forming the infundibulum and fimbriae. The caudal parts fuse into the uterovaginal canal, which forms the body and cervix of the uterus and the upper vagina. As the ducts move medially they raise a transverse peritoneal fold, the broad ligament. The solid tip of the canal reaches the posterior wall of the urogenital sinus at the sinus tubercle and induces the sinovaginal bulbs, which form a solid vaginal plate that later canalizes into the lower vagina; the hymen marks the junction. A single uterine cavity therefore requires three steps in order: growth of both ducts, fusion in the midline, and resorption of the septum left where their walls meet.

blocks.title: Building one uterus from two ducts
steps: Paramesonephric ducts form lateral to the mesonephric ducts
Cranial unfused parts become the uterine tubes
Caudal parts fuse into the uterovaginal canal
Midline septum resorbs, leaving one cavity
Canal meets sinovaginal bulbs; vaginal plate canalizes
blocks.caption: Failure of growth, fusion, or resorption produces a distinct malformation.

blocks.text: The defect identifies the step that failed. If the ducts never fuse, each forms its own uterus and cervix (uterus didelphys), often with a longitudinal vaginal septum. If fusion is incomplete at the fundus, two horns remain with an indented outer contour (bicornuate uterus). If fusion is complete but the septum persists, the outer fundal contour is smooth while a fibromuscular wall divides the cavity (septate uterus), the most common of these anomalies. The septum is relatively poorly vascularized and an embryo implanting on it is more likely to be lost, so septate uterus carries the highest risk of recurrent pregnancy loss among them. If one duct fails to grow, a single horn results (unicornuate uterus); if both fail, the uterus and upper vagina are absent (Mullerian agenesis, Mayer-Rokitansky-Kuster-Hauser syndrome).

blocks.title: Mullerian anomalies by failed step
rows: Two cavities, two cervices, often a vaginal septum
Cavity divided by a septum; one cervix
blocks.caption: An outer notch means a fusion problem; a smooth outside with a wall inside means a resorption problem.

blocks.text: Two consequences follow from the anatomy. The ovaries arise from the gonadal ridge, not the ducts, so ovarian estrogen, breast development, and pubic hair are normal; Mullerian agenesis presents as primary amenorrhea in a 46,XX woman with normal secondary sex characteristics. The mesonephric duct both guides the paramesonephric duct and gives off the ureteric bud, so renal agenesis or a pelvic kidney often accompanies these defects, typically on the side of a missing horn.

The external genitalia begin identically in both sexes. In weeks 3 to 4, mesenchyme around the cloacal membrane forms the cloacal folds, which meet cranially as the genital tubercle. When the urorectal septum reaches the cloacal membrane at about the end of week 6, the folds divide into the urethral (urogenital) folds in front and the anal folds behind, and a second pair of elevations, the labioscrotal (genital) swellings, appears lateral to the urethral folds. Differences appear in about week 9, and the genitalia are clearly male or female by about week 12. Whether the primordia follow the male or the female path depends on DHT acting through the androgen receptor, not on the karyotype.

In the male, DHT makes the genital tubercle elongate into the phallus, which pulls the urethral folds forward to form the walls of the urethral groove over the endodermal urethral plate. The folds then fuse over the groove from proximal to distal, closing the spongy (penile) urethra and leaving the penile raphe on the ventral surface; the urethra in the glans is completed last. The labioscrotal swellings enlarge, move caudally, and fuse in the midline as the scrotum, marked by the scrotal raphe.

In the female, without DHT, the genital tubercle elongates only slightly to form the clitoris, the urethral folds stay separate as the labia minora, and the labioscrotal swellings stay separate as the labia majora, joined in front at the mons pubis and behind at the posterior labial commissure. The urogenital groove remains open as the vestibule, which receives the urethra and vagina.

blocks.title: Indifferent primordia and their derivatives
rows: Glans clitoris and corpora of the clitoris
Ventral penile shaft enclosing the spongy (penile) urethra
Prostate, bulbourethral glands, prostatic and membranous urethra
Paraurethral (Skene) glands, greater vestibular (Bartholin) glands, lower vagina, urethra
blocks.caption: Structures in the same row are homologues. Fusion in the male and non-fusion in the female explain each pair.

blocks.text: Timing and site explain the common errors. Androgen exposure of a 46,XX fetus, most often from 21-hydroxylase deficiency, before about week 12 fuses the labioscrotal swellings and urethral folds, whereas exposure after that time can only enlarge the clitoris. In hypospadias, the most common penile anomaly, the urethral folds fail to fuse completely, so the urethra opens on the ventral surface anywhere from the glans to the perineum; deficient androgen production or action is one cause, and cryptorchidism often coexists. Epispadias is a different error: the genital tubercle forms too far caudally, near the urorectal septum, so the urethral opening lies on the dorsal surface. It often accompanies bladder exstrophy, a defect of the ventral body wall.

sections.title: Testicular descent, the processus vaginalis, and inguinal defects

blocks.text: The testis develops high on the posterior abdominal wall, beside the mesonephros, and keeps the vessels and lymphatics it acquired there. The testicular artery arises from the abdominal aorta below the renal arteries, the left testicular vein drains to the left renal vein, and testicular lymph drains to para-aortic nodes, whereas scrotal skin drains to superficial inguinal nodes.

The gubernaculum is a mesenchymal cord running from the lower pole of the testis through the developing abdominal wall to the labioscrotal swelling. Descent has two phases. In the transabdominal phase (about weeks 8 to 15), insulin-like peptide 3 (INSL3) from Leydig cells makes the gubernaculum swell, holding the testis near the future deep inguinal ring while the lumbar region grows away from it. In the inguinoscrotal phase (about weeks 25 to 35), androgen-dependent migration of the gubernaculum draws the testis through the inguinal canal into the scrotum, usually by birth. The scrotum keeps the testis about 2 to 3 °C (3.6 to 5.4 °F) below core temperature, which spermatogenesis requires, so an undescended testis (cryptorchidism, about 3% of term boys and more of preterm boys) has impaired spermatogenesis and a higher risk of germ cell tumors.

blocks.caption: The testis passes behind the processus vaginalis, so the tunica vaginalis covers its front and sides.

blocks.text: Ahead of the testis, a pouch of peritoneum, the processus vaginalis, evaginates along the gubernaculum, and each abdominal wall layer it passes through forms a covering of the spermatic cord. After descent the connection between the processus and the peritoneal cavity normally closes, at about birth or within the first year, leaving the tunica vaginalis as a closed serous sac.

blocks.title: Abdominal wall layers and the coverings they form
cols: Covering of the cord and testis
rows: No covering; it arches over the canal
blocks.caption: An indirect hernia follows the same route and acquires all three spermatic fasciae.

blocks.text: If the processus stays open, the width of the channel decides what can follow it. A wide channel admits bowel or omentum, producing an indirect (congenital) inguinal hernia that enters the deep ring lateral to the inferior epigastric vessels and runs within the spermatic cord, sometimes into the scrotum. It is the most common groin hernia in both sexes. A narrow channel admits only peritoneal fluid, producing a communicating hydrocele. In the female, the gubernaculum becomes the ovarian ligament and the round ligament of the uterus, and a patent processus (canal of Nuck) can produce an indirect hernia or hydrocele into the labium majus.

blocks.title: Inguinal and scrotal swellings compared

Size varies through the day; transilluminates

blocks.caption: Indirect hernia and communicating hydrocele are the same embryologic defect differing only in width.

blocks.predict: A 2-year-old has a scrotal swelling that transilluminates, is small each morning, and enlarges by evening. What structure is open, and why does bowel not enter it?
blocks.explain: A narrow patent processus vaginalis lets peritoneal fluid drain down when upright and return when supine (communicating hydrocele). It is too narrow for bowel; a wider channel gives an indirect hernia.

blocks.text: The placenta has a fetal part, the chorion frondosum, and a maternal part, the decidua basalis. Placental formation begins at implantation (about days 6 to 8 after fertilization), when the trophoblast differentiates into two layers. The inner cytotrophoblast is mononuclear and mitotically active, a stem layer. The outer syncytiotrophoblast forms by fusion of cytotrophoblast cells; it is multinucleated, does not divide, invades the endometrium, and is the endocrine layer that secretes hCG, which keeps the corpus luteum making progesterone until the placenta takes over at about weeks 8 to 12. By about day 12, lacunae in the syncytium open into eroded maternal sinusoids, starting the uteroplacental circulation.

blocks.caption: Once tertiary villi connect to the embryonic heart, exchange with maternal blood can begin.

blocks.text: Villi at first cover the whole chorion. As the embryo grows, villi beneath the thinning decidua capsularis lose their blood supply and degenerate, leaving the smooth chorion laeve, while villi facing the decidua basalis branch richly as the chorion frondosum. Decidual cells, enlarged endometrial stromal cells filled with glycogen and lipid, limit trophoblast invasion; where decidua basalis is deficient, as over a prior uterine scar, villi attach to or invade the myometrium (placenta accreta spectrum).

blocks.caption: Umbilical vessels are named by direction relative to the fetal heart, not by oxygen content.

blocks.text: By the fourth month the placenta has a fetal chorionic plate and a maternal basal plate. Decidual septa divide the maternal surface into about 15 to 20 cotyledons. Maternal blood from the spiral arteries fills the intervillous space and bathes the villi directly, so the human placenta is hemochorial, yet fetal and maternal blood do not mix. They are separated by the placental membrane, which late in pregnancy thins to syncytiotrophoblast, a discontinuous cytotrophoblast, basal lamina, connective tissue, and fetal capillary endothelium. Extravillous cytotrophoblast remodels the spiral arteries into wide, low-resistance vessels; shallow remodeling is a central mechanism of preeclampsia (RE-13-H). At term the placenta weighs about 500 to 600 g.

The umbilical cord forms from the connecting stalk and is covered by amnion. It normally holds two umbilical arteries and one umbilical vein (the left; the right regresses early) in Wharton jelly, a mucoid connective tissue rich in hyaluronic acid that cushions the vessels, together with remnants of the allantois and vitelline duct. A single umbilical artery, found in about 1% of cords, is associated with renal, cardiac, and chromosomal anomalies, notably trisomy 18.

blocks.predict: In placenta accreta, which layer is missing, and why does the placenta fail to separate after delivery?
blocks.explain: The decidua basalis is deficient, so villi anchor directly in the myometrium. Normal separation occurs within the decidua basalis; without it there is no cleavage plane.

sections.title: Breast development and the milk line

blocks.text: The breast is a modified apocrine sweat gland: its ducts and alveoli come from surface ectoderm, and its stroma and fat from the underlying mesoderm. Early in the second month, a band of thickened ectoderm, the mammary ridge or milk line, appears on each side of the ventral body wall, running from the axilla to the inguinal region.

Most of the ridge then regresses. Only a short segment over the pectoral region persists and sinks into the mesenchyme as a primary bud, which sends out about 15 to 20 secondary sprouts. These canalize late in fetal life to form the lactiferous ducts, each draining one lobe. At birth the ducts open into a shallow epithelial pit, which proliferation of the underlying mesenchyme raises into the nipple; failure of this eversion leaves an inverted nipple.

blocks.caption: A failure of regression anywhere along the ridge leaves accessory nipple or breast tissue on that line.

blocks.text: Until puberty the breast in both sexes is a small branched duct system. A newborn's breasts may swell and secrete a little milk for a few weeks because maternal estrogen crossed the placenta, then regress as it falls. At puberty, ovarian estrogen drives duct elongation, branching, and stromal growth, progesterone adds lobuloalveolar development, and full secretory differentiation waits for pregnancy (RE-6).

Any segment of the ridge that fails to regress can form a nipple (supernumerary nipple, polythelia) or glandular tissue (polymastia) anywhere along the line from axilla to groin. Accessory nipples most often lie on the chest or upper abdomen below the normal breast and are easily mistaken for nevi, while accessory glandular tissue is most common in the axilla. Because it is true breast tissue, it responds to hormones, swelling before menstruation and during pregnancy and lactation, and it can develop the same diseases as the normal breast, including fibroadenoma and carcinoma. Absence of the breast (amastia) or nipple (athelia) is rare and may accompany absence of the pectoralis major in Poland syndrome.

integration.text: Anatomy, physiology, and genetics meet in this chapter. The gonad's location on the posterior abdominal wall explains the aortic origin of the testicular artery, the left testicular vein draining to the renal vein, and para-aortic spread of testicular tumors. The intermediate mesoderm builds both the urinary and genital systems, so the mesonephric duct links renal agenesis to Mullerian anomalies. Biochemistry decides the phenotype: SRY and SOX9 are transcription factors, AMH is a TGF-beta ligand, testosterone and DHT share one nuclear receptor, and 21-hydroxylase or 5-alpha-reductase deficiency changes anatomy by changing which steroid reaches which tissue.

Pathology follows from each failed step. Streak gonads with Y material give germ cell tumors, cryptorchid testes give infertility and tumors, a patent processus gives hernias and hydroceles, shallow trophoblast invasion gives preeclampsia and excessive invasion gives accreta, and persistent ridge tissue develops ordinary breast disease. The models here are simplified: the ovarian pathway is active rather than passive, the origin of the vagina is still debated, and timing values vary between texts, so reason from the sequence of steps rather than exact weeks.

summary: SRY on Yp switches on SOX9, which makes Sertoli cells and a testis; without SRY an actively maintained ovary forms.
46,XY with SRY deletion gives streak gonads and female anatomy; 46,XX with SRY translocation gives small azoospermic testes and a male phenotype.
Sertoli cell AMH removes the Mullerian ducts; Leydig cell testosterone keeps the Wolffian ducts by local action; DHT builds the penis, scrotum, and prostate.
Androgen insensitivity gives testes, no uterus, and female external genitalia; 5-alpha-reductase deficiency gives male ducts with ambiguous genitalia.
Mullerian ducts form the tubes, uterus, cervix, and upper vagina; the lower vagina comes from the urogenital sinus.
No fusion gives didelphys, partial fusion gives bicornuate, and failed septum resorption gives septate uterus, the type with the most pregnancy loss.
Genital tubercle, urogenital folds, and labioscrotal swellings give the glans, ventral shaft and spongy urethra, and scrotum in males, and the clitoris, labia minora, and labia majora in females.
Hypospadias is ventral from unfused urogenital folds; epispadias is dorsal from a misplaced genital tubercle.
The gubernaculum guides the testis through the inguinal canal; a wide patent processus vaginalis gives an indirect hernia and a narrow one a communicating hydrocele.
Chorion frondosum and decidua basalis form the placenta; the cord holds two arteries and one vein in Wharton jelly; extra nipples lie on the milk line from axilla to groin.

verify: Timing values (bipotential gonad until about week 7, AMH window about weeks 8 to 10, labioscrotal fusion before about week 12, descent phases about weeks 8 to 15 and 25 to 35) vary between Langman, Moore, and review sources; confirm what NABNE expects.

Some sources date the appearance of the mammary ridge to week 4 and others to weeks 6 to 7; this chapter says early in the second month. Sprout number is given as 15 to 20 here and 16 to 24 in Langman.
The origin of the upper vagina (uterovaginal canal versus urogenital sinus for the whole vagina) differs between sources; this chapter follows the dual-origin model in Langman.
The explanation that septate uterus causes pregnancy loss through a poorly vascularized septum is classic teaching but has been questioned; the higher loss rate itself is consistent across sources.
Frequencies quoted (cryptorchidism about 3% of term boys, single umbilical artery about 1%, placental weight about 500 to 600 g) are approximate consensus values.

Confirm whether NABNE expects eponyms such as Swyer syndrome, Mayer-Rokitansky-Kuster-Hauser syndrome, Gartner duct, canal of Nuck, Hesselbach triangle, and Poland syndrome, or only the descriptive terms.

Requested new diagram names for a future revision: sex-differentiation (indifferent gonad and duct pairs to male and female outcomes), mullerian-anomalies (didelphys, bicornuate, septate, unicornuate outlines), external-genitalia-homologues, testicular-descent (three positions with processus vaginalis, hernia, and hydrocele), and placenta-villus (cross-section of a tertiary villus and intervillous space).
